title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Note



Draft for review. All four examples are in; examples 03 and 04 do not have a Reactant column yet. Plan and status: AGENTS.md.
“Why do you use Julia instead of JAX?” is a fair question, and “JAX can’t sort” is the wrong answer: jax.lax.sort is differentiable. The real difference is the execution model.
JAX differentiates pure functions over fixed-shape arrays with a static computation graph. Anything that fits that model runs well, often better than hand-written code, because XLA fuses and vectorises it. Enzyme differentiates the imperative program as written, including in-place mutation, data-dependent loop bounds and growing buffers. When an algorithm’s efficient form is irregular, JAX makes you regularise it with padding, masks, static trip counts or implicit differentiation. Enzyme lets you keep it.
Each example below implements the same loss three times, with Enzyme.jl, with Reactant.jl, and with JAX, checks that all three give the same gradient, and times them on a CUDA GPU. Reactant is the control: it is Julia compiled through XLA, the same static-graph model as JAX. Where Reactant hits the same wall as JAX, the cause is the execution model, not the language.

title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Where the gap shows up

Data-dependent output size or sparsity

Compaction and filtering (x[mask], push!), sparse assembly with data-dependent fill-in, contact detection, tree codes (octrees, Barnes–Hut). JAX needs a static upper bound and masks. → 03. Compaction

Data-dependent control flow

Iterative solvers with convergence tests, adaptive time stepping. JAX cannot reverse-differentiate lax.while_loop, so you fix the iteration count or switch to implicit differentiation. → 04. Newton

Sequential in-place updates

Gauss–Seidel, SOR, Thomas algorithm, sweeps where element i depends on the just-updated i−1. In JAX these become lax.scan loops with one XLA step per element, and for nonlinear updates reverse mode stores every carry unless you rematerialise. → 02. Gauss–Seidel

Irregular neighbour access

Particle methods with cell lists (sort by cell, loop over a data-dependent number of neighbours), scatter-accumulate with data-dependent indices, histogramming, resampling. → 01. Particles

title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Where JAX wins
Dense, batched, regular work: most of machine learning, many PDE stencils, anything whose naive cost already equals its smart cost. There the regularised JAX version is often faster despite padding, because XLA fuses and the hardware wants regular access. And the advantage on this site is Enzyme’s, not Julia’s: Julia AD tools that do not support mutation (Zygote) cannot do this either.

title: 04. Newton’s method: a loop that stops when it has converged
text:
Solve the nonlinear boundary-value problem \[F(u, \theta) = A u + u^3 - \theta = 0, \qquad A = \tfrac{1}{h^2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1, 2, -1),\] by Newton’s method until the step is small, \(\lVert\delta\rVert_\infty \le 10^{-10}\lVert u\rVert_\infty\), and differentiate \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \lVert u^\ast(\theta) - u_{\text{obs}}\rVert^2\) with respect to \(\theta\). Each Newton step solves a tridiagonal system with the Thomas algorithm, a sequential in-place sweep.
Two irregular patterns:

Data-dependent control flow. The number of Newton steps depends on \(\theta\) (3–4 here).
Sequential in-place update. The Thomas forward elimination and back substitution.

text:
Code

Enzyme.jlJAX




"Residual F(u, θ) = A u + u³ − θ with zero Dirichlet ends, written into F."
function residual!(F, u, θ)
    n = length(u)
    ih2 = (n + 1)^2
    for i in 1:n
        l = i > 1 ? u[i-1] : zero(eltype(u))
        r = i < n ? u[i+1] : zero(eltype(u))
        F[i] = ih2 * (2u[i] - l - r) + u[i]^3 - θ[i]
    end
end

"Solve J δ = F in place (δ overwrites F), J = A + 3 diag(u²): the Thomas algorithm."
function thomas!(F, c, u)
    n = length(u)
    ih2 = (n + 1)^2
    off = -ih2
    b = 2ih2 + 3u[1]^2
    c[1] = off / b
    F[1] = F[1] / b
    for i in 2:n                                  # forward elimination
        b = 2ih2 + 3u[i]^2 - off * c[i-1]
        c[i] = off / b
        F[i] = (F[i] - off * F[i-1]) / b
    end
    for i in n-1:-1:1                             # back substitution
        F[i] -= c[i] * F[i+1]
    end
end

"Newton until the step is small; returns the solution and the iteration count."
function newton_solve(θ::AbstractVector{T}) where {T}
    n = length(θ)
    u, F, c = zeros(T, n), zeros(T, n), zeros(T, n)
    it, converged = 0, false
    while !converged && it < MAXITER              # data-dependent trip count
        residual!(F, u, θ)
        thomas!(F, c, u)                          # F now holds the Newton step δ
        u .-= F
        it += 1
        converged = maximum(abs, F) <= TOL * maximum(abs, u)
    end
    return u, it
end

newton_loss(θ, uobs) = sum(abs2, first(newton_solve(θ)) .- uobs)

newton_loss (generic function with 1 method)


Source: 04. Newton solver — Enzyme.jl


"Reverse mode straight through the while loop, the Newton steps and the Thomas sweeps."
function newton_gradient(θ, uobs)
    dθ = zero(θ)
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, newton_loss, Active, Duplicated(θ, dθ), Const(uobs))
    return dθ
end

g = newton_gradient(θ0, uobs0)

Implicit-function alternative:


# The alternative a numerical analyst would choose: at the solution, F(u*, θ) = 0, so
# dL/dθ = λ with Jᵀλ = ∂L/∂u (J is symmetric here). One tridiagonal solve, no tape.
function newton_gradient_implicit(θ, uobs)
    u, _ = newton_solve(θ)
    λ, c = 2 .* (u .- uobs), similar(u)
    thomas!(λ, c, u)
    return λ
end

g_imp = newton_gradient_implicit(θ0, uobs0)
@printf "unrolled vs implicit: max rel. difference %.1e\n" maximum(abs, g - g_imp) / maximum(abs, g)

unrolled vs implicit: max rel. difference 2.6e-14







def residual(u, theta):
    n = u.shape[0]
    ih2 = (n + 1) ** 2
    up = jnp.pad(u, 1)
    return ih2 * (2 * u - up[:-2] - up[2:]) + u**3 - theta

def newton_step(u, theta):
    n = u.shape[0]
    ih2 = (n + 1) ** 2
    lower = jnp.full(n, -ih2, u.dtype).at[0].set(0.0)
    upper = jnp.full(n, -ih2, u.dtype).at[-1].set(0.0)
    diag = 2 * ih2 + 3 * u**2
    delta = jax.lax.linalg.tridiagonal_solve(lower, diag, upper, residual(u, theta)[:, None])[:, 0]
    return u - delta

# The direct translation: Newton until the step is small.
def loss_while(theta, uobs):
    def cond(state):
        u, step, it = state
        return (step > TOL * jnp.max(jnp.abs(u))) & (it < MAXITER)
    def body(state):
        u, _, it = state
        u_new = newton_step(u, theta)
        return u_new, jnp.max(jnp.abs(u_new - u)), it + 1
    u, _, _ = jax.lax.while_loop(cond, body, (jnp.zeros_like(theta), jnp.inf, 0))
    return jnp.sum((u - uobs) ** 2)

# Workaround 1: a fixed number of Newton steps, enough for the worst case.
def loss_fixed(theta, uobs, iters=MAXITER):
    u = jax.lax.fori_loop(0, iters, lambda _, u: newton_step(u, theta), jnp.zeros_like(theta))
    return jnp.sum((u - uobs) ** 2)

# Workaround 2 (idiomatic): Optimistix root finding, differentiated implicitly.
def loss_implicit(theta, uobs):
    # Optimistix stops when the step is small *and* |F| < atol. Rounding in F grows like
    # (n+1)²·eps, so we root-find on h²·F instead: same root, same Newton steps, same
    # implicit gradient, but a residual whose rounding error is ~eps·|u|.
    def scaled_residual(u, theta):
        return residual(u, theta) / (u.shape[0] + 1) ** 2
    solver = optx.Newton(rtol=TOL, atol=1e-12, linear_solver=lx.Tridiagonal())
    sol = optx.root_find(scaled_residual, solver, jnp.zeros_like(theta), theta,
                         tags=frozenset({lx.tridiagonal_tag}), max_steps=MAXITER)
    return jnp.sum((sol.value - uobs) ** 2)

Differentiating through the iterations stores every Newton step for the reverse pass. That costs time and memory (at \(n = 10^6\), Enzyme allocates 69 MiB unrolled against 38 MiB implicit), and it is the reason JAX refuses dynamic loops. Implicit differentiation is usually the better method anyway, and the table shows that.
The fixed-count workaround is expensive: it has to run the worst case (here MAXITER = 50 steps) although Newton converges in 3–4, and reverse mode then stores all 50. Choosing a smaller count means guessing how many steps every future input will need. The difference is who decides. With Enzyme it is a choice: the loop as written works, and the implicit adjoint is a few lines when you want it. With JAX you are forced into implicit differentiation or fixed iteration counts, and for a solver without a clean fixed-point structure (adaptive time stepping, line searches, event detection) there may be no implicit formulation to fall back on.

Where JAX wins / what we did not do






Note



On the GPU, JAX with Optimistix’s implicit differentiation is by far the fastest: 3.5 ms at \(n = 10^6\), using XLA’s GPU tridiagonal solver. Enzyme’s version here is single-threaded CPU code.
Using Optimistix did take care: its default stopping test requires \(|F| <\) atol, which rounding makes unreachable for this problem at large \(n\), and its alternative step-based test reports “diverged” once the steps stall at rounding level. The fix, root-finding on the rescaled residual \(h^2 F\), is in the JAX code above.



No Enzyme GPU version. The Thomas algorithm is sequential, so a GPU version would need a different tridiagonal solver (cyclic reduction) on both sides.

import functools
import numpy as np
import weanj  # sets XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false before JAX initialises
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
EXAMPLE = "03-compaction"
T, DT, HW, NB = 50, 0.01, 0.005, 1024  # steps, time step, window half-width, bins
d = weanj.load_inputs(EXAMPLE)
x0, v0, target0 = (jnp.asarray(d[k]) for k in ("x0", "v", "target"))


def minimg(d):
    return d - jnp.round(d)

def taper(d):
    return jnp.maximum(1.0 - jnp.abs(d) / HW, 0.0) ** 2

def deposit(H, x, w):
    """Cloud-in-cell scatter-add into the histogram."""
    g = x * NB - 0.5
    j = jnp.floor(g).astype(jnp.int32)
    f = g - j
    return H.at[j % NB].add(w * (1 - f)).at[(j + 1) % NB].add(w * f)

# Masked: every particle is deposited at every step, with weight 0 outside the window.
@jax.jit
def loss_masked(x0, v, target):
    def step(H, t):
        x = x0 + v * (t * DT)
        d = minimg(x - t / T)
        w = jnp.where(jnp.abs(d) < HW, taper(d), 0.0)
        return deposit(H, x - jnp.floor(x), w), None
    H, _ = jax.lax.scan(step, jnp.zeros(NB, x0.dtype), jnp.arange(1, T + 1))
    return jnp.sum((H - target) ** 2)

# Compacted: the closest JAX gets to x[mask]. `nonzero` needs a static `size`, so the
# selection is padded to a capacity chosen from the data, checked outside jit.
@functools.partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=3)
def loss_compact(x0, v, target, cap):
    n = x0.shape[0]
    def step(H, t):
        inside = jnp.abs(minimg(x0 + v * (t * DT) - t / T)) < HW
        idx = jnp.nonzero(inside, size=cap, fill_value=n)[0]
        i = jnp.minimum(idx, n - 1)
        x = x0[i] + v[i] * (t * DT)
        w = jnp.where(idx < n, taper(minimg(x - t / T)), 0.0)
        return deposit(H, x - jnp.floor(x), w), None
    H, _ = jax.lax.scan(step, jnp.zeros(NB, x0.dtype), jnp.arange(1, T + 1))
    return jnp.sum((H - target) ** 2)

def needed_capacity(x0, v):
    """Largest number of selected particles at any step (host-side, outside jit)."""
    t = np.arange(1, T + 1)[:, None]
    d = np.asarray(x0)[None] + np.asarray(v)[None] * t * DT - t / T
    return int((np.abs(d - np.round(d)) < HW).sum(axis=1).max())


grad_masked = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss_masked))
grad_compact = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss_compact), static_argnums=3)

cap0 = needed_capacity(x0, v0)
g = grad_compact(x0, v0, target0, cap0)
print(f"capacity = {cap0}   loss = {float(loss_compact(x0, v0, target0, cap0)):.10f}   "
      f"‖∇loss‖ = {float(jnp.linalg.norm(g)):.6f}")

err = weanj.fd_check(lambda y: loss_compact(jnp.asarray(y), v0, target0, cap0), np.asarray(x0), np.asarray(g), n=20, h=1e-7)

using WEANJ, Enzyme, CUDA, KernelAbstractions, Printf
include("common.jl")   # Setup, wrap, minimg, taper, inputs

Setup{Float64}(50, 0.01, 0.005, 1024)



function deposit_loss(x0::Vector{T}, v, target, s::Setup) where {T}
    N, nb = length(x0), s.nb
    H = zeros(T, nb)
    sel = Int[]                                   # grows and shrinks with the data
    for t in 1:s.T
        c = T(t) / s.T                            # window centre
        empty!(sel)
        for i in 1:N                              # compaction: indices of x[mask]
            d = minimg(x0[i] + v[i] * (t * s.dt) - c)
            abs(d) < s.halfwidth && push!(sel, i)
        end
        for i in sel                              # work only for the selected particles
            x = wrap(x0[i] + v[i] * (t * s.dt))
            w = taper(minimg(x - c), s.halfwidth)
            g = x * nb - T(0.5)                   # cloud-in-cell deposit
            j = floor(Int, g)
            f = g - j
            H[mod(j, nb) + 1] += w * (1 - f)      # scatter-add at a data-dependent index
            H[mod(j + 1, nb) + 1] += w * f
        end
    end
    return sum(abs2, H .- target)
end

deposit_loss (generic function with 1 method)



function deposit_gradient(x0::Vector, v, target, s)
    dx = zero(x0)
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, deposit_loss, Active, Duplicated(x0, dx), Const(v), Const(target), Const(s))
    return dx
end

# On the GPU the natural form is one thread per particle and step: threads outside the
# window return immediately, the rest scatter into H with atomic adds.
Enzyme.EnzymeRules.inactive_type(::Type{<:Setup}) = true   # constants, never differentiated

@kernel function deposit_step!(H, @Const(x0), @Const(v), s, t)
    i = @index(Global)
    T = eltype(H)
    @inbounds begin
        x = wrap(x0[i] + v[i] * (t * s.dt))
        d = minimg(x - T(t) / s.T)
        if abs(d) < s.halfwidth
            w = taper(d, s.halfwidth)
            g = x * s.nb - T(0.5)
            j = unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(g))
            f = g - j
            KernelAbstractions.@atomic H[mod(j, Int32(s.nb)) + 1] += w * (1 - f)
            KernelAbstractions.@atomic H[mod(j + Int32(1), Int32(s.nb)) + 1] += w * f
        end
    end
end

function deposit!(H, x0, v, s)
    fill!(H, 0)
    for t in 1:s.T
        deposit_step!(get_backend(H))(H, x0, v, s, t; ndrange=length(x0))
    end
    return nothing
end

function deposit_loss(x0::CuVector, v, target, s)
    H = similar(x0, s.nb)
    deposit!(H, x0, v, s)
    return sum(abs2, H .- target)
end

"Reverse through deposit!, seeded with ∂loss/∂H = 2(H − target)."
function deposit_gradient(x0::CuVector{T}, v, target, s) where {T}
    H = similar(x0, s.nb)
    deposit!(H, x0, v, s)
    dH = 2 .* (H .- target)
    dx = CUDA.zeros(T, length(x0))
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, deposit!, Const, Duplicated(H, dH), Duplicated(x0, dx), Const(v), Const(s))
    return dx
end

import functools
import numpy as np
import weanj  # sets XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false before JAX initialises
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

EXAMPLE, K_CHECK = "02-gauss-seidel", 20

# Lexicographic Gauss–Seidel. Arrays are immutable and loop bodies must be pure, so
# the sweep is a scan over columns, each a scan over rows carrying the new u[i-1, j].
# Same update order as the Julia loop (i fastest, then j).
@functools.partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=2)
def gs_loss(theta, uobs, K):
    n = theta.shape[0]
    h2 = 1.0 / (n + 1) ** 2

    def column(u, j):
        left, old, right = u[:, j], u[:, j + 1], u[:, j + 2]

        def point(below, i):  # below = new u[i-1, j]
            new = (h2 * theta[i, j] + below + old[i + 2] + left[i + 1] + right[i + 1]) / 4
            return new, new

        _, col = jax.lax.scan(point, old[0], jnp.arange(n))
        return u.at[1:n + 1, j + 1].set(col), None

    def sweep(u, _):
        return jax.lax.scan(column, u, jnp.arange(n))[0], None

    u, _ = jax.lax.scan(sweep, jnp.zeros((n + 2, n + 2), theta.dtype), None, length=K)
    return jnp.sum((u[1:-1, 1:-1] - uobs) ** 2)


gs_grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(gs_loss), static_argnums=2)
g_lex = gs_grad(theta0, uobs0, K_CHECK)
print(f"loss = {float(gs_loss(theta0, uobs0, K_CHECK)):.12f}   ‖∇loss‖ = {float(jnp.linalg.norm(g_lex)):.6e}")

loss = 0.105860373742   ‖∇loss‖ = 6.409859e-04



# Red-black Gauss–Seidel: the reformulation JAX users actually write. Each colour is
# one vectorised stencil, selected with a mask.
@functools.partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=2)
def rb_loss(theta, uobs, K):
    n = theta.shape[0]
    h2 = 1.0 / (n + 1) ** 2
    i, j = jnp.meshgrid(jnp.arange(2, n + 2), jnp.arange(2, n + 2), indexing="ij")
    red = (i + j) % 2 == 0  # 1-based indices, as in the Julia kernel

    def half(u, colour):
        new = (h2 * theta + u[:-2, 1:-1] + u[2:, 1:-1] + u[1:-1, :-2] + u[1:-1, 2:]) / 4
        return u.at[1:-1, 1:-1].set(jnp.where(colour, new, u[1:-1, 1:-1]))

    def sweep(u, _):
        return half(half(u, red), ~red), None

    u, _ = jax.lax.scan(sweep, jnp.zeros((n + 2, n + 2), theta.dtype), None, length=K)
    return jnp.sum((u[1:-1, 1:-1] - uobs) ** 2)


rb_grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(rb_loss), static_argnums=2)
g_rb = rb_grad(theta0, uobs0, K_CHECK)

def temp_bytes(fn, *args):

# Lexicographic Gauss–Seidel, in place: u[i, j] uses the *new* u[i-1, j] and u[i, j-1].
function gs_loss(θ::AbstractMatrix{T}, uobs, K) where {T}
    n = size(θ, 1)
    h2 = one(T) / (n + 1)^2
    u = zeros(T, n + 2, n + 2)
    for _ in 1:K, j in 2:n+1, i in 2:n+1
        u[i, j] = (h2 * θ[i-1, j-1] + u[i-1, j] + u[i+1, j] + u[i, j-1] + u[i, j+1]) / 4
    end
    loss = zero(T)
    for j in 1:n, i in 1:n
        loss += (u[i+1, j+1] - uobs[i, j])^2
    end
    return loss
end

function gs_gradient(θ, uobs, K)
    dθ = zero(θ)
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, gs_loss, Active, Duplicated(θ, dθ), Const(uobs), Const(K))

# Red-black Gauss–Seidel as a KernelAbstractions kernel (runs on CPU and GPU): points
# of one colour read only the other colour, so all threads of a colour are independent.
@kernel function rb_half_sweep!(u, @Const(θ), colour)
    I = @index(Global, Cartesian)
    i, j = I[1] + 1, I[2] + 1
    h2 = one(eltype(u)) / (size(θ, 1) + 1)^2   # computed here: GPU kernels take no active scalars
    @inbounds if (i + j) % 2 == colour
        u[i, j] = (h2 * θ[i-1, j-1] + u[i-1, j] + u[i+1, j] + u[i, j-1] + u[i, j+1]) / 4
    end
end

@kernel function sqdiff!(e, @Const(u), @Const(uobs))
    I = @index(Global, Cartesian)
    @inbounds e[I] = (u[I[1]+1, I[2]+1] - uobs[I])^2
end

"Loss terms e (the loss is sum(e)); u is the in-place solution buffer."
function rb_terms!(e, u, θ, uobs, K)
    backend, n = get_backend(u), size(θ, 1)
    fill!(u, 0)
    for _ in 1:K, colour in (0, 1)
        rb_half_sweep!(backend)(u, θ, colour; ndrange=(n, n))
    end
    sqdiff!(backend)(e, u, uobs; ndrange=(n, n))
    return nothing
end

function rb_loss(θ, uobs, K)
    n = size(θ, 1)
    e, u = similar(θ), similar(θ, n + 2, n + 2)
    rb_terms!(e, u, θ, uobs, K)
    return sum(e)
end

function rb_gradient(θ, uobs, K)
    n = size(θ, 1)
    e, de = similar(θ), fill!(similar(θ), 1)
    u, du = similar(θ, n + 2, n + 2), fill!(similar(θ, n + 2, n + 2), 0)
    dθ = fill!(similar(θ), 0)
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, rb_terms!, Const, Duplicated(e, de), Duplicated(u, du),
                    Duplicated(θ, dθ), Const(uobs), Const(K))
    return dθ

import math
import numpy as np
import weanj  # sets XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false before JAX initialises
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax_md import partition, space

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
EXAMPLE = "01-particles"
x0 = jnp.asarray(weanj.load_inputs(EXAMPLE)["x"].T)  # (N, 2); Julia stores 2×N


# Idiomatic JAX: jax-md's neighbour list. It is a fixed-capacity padded pair list;
# `allocate` (outside jit) sizes it from the data, `update` (inside jit) refills it,
# and `did_buffer_overflow` must be checked after every call.
NUMBER_DENSITY, H, MASS = 10.0, 0.5, 1.0
RC, RHO0 = 2 * H, NUMBER_DENSITY

def box_size(n):
    return math.sqrt(n / NUMBER_DENSITY)

def W(r, h=H):
    """2D cubic spline. No `if`: both branches are evaluated and selected."""
    q = r / h
    sigma = 10.0 / (7.0 * math.pi * h * h)
    t = jnp.maximum(2.0 - q, 0.0)
    return sigma * jnp.where(q < 1.0, 1.0 - 1.5 * q**2 + 0.75 * q**3, 0.25 * t**3)

def make_loss(n, displacement):
    w0 = MASS * float(W(0.0))  # self-contribution; jax-md's pair list excludes i == j

    def loss(x, nbrs):
        nbrs = nbrs.update(x)  # rebuild the cell list from the current positions
        i, j = nbrs.idx
        mask = i < n  # padded slots hold index n
        dR = jax.vmap(displacement)(x[i], x[j])
        dR = jnp.where(mask[:, None], dR, 1.0)  # padded dR = 0 would make ∇‖dR‖ NaN
        r = jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(dR**2, axis=1))
        w = jnp.where(mask, MASS * W(r), 0.0)
        rho = w0 + jax.ops.segment_sum(w, i, num_segments=n)
        return jnp.sum((rho - RHO0) ** 2), nbrs

    return loss

class Particles:
    """Jitted loss and gradient with jax-md's overflow-and-reallocate protocol."""

    def __init__(self, x, capacity_multiplier=1.25):
        self.n = x.shape[0]
        L = box_size(self.n)
        displacement, _ = space.periodic(L)
        self.neighbor_fn = partition.neighbor_list(
            displacement, L, RC, dr_threshold=0.0,
            capacity_multiplier=capacity_multiplier, format=partition.Sparse)
        self.nbrs = self.neighbor_fn.allocate(x)
        loss = make_loss(self.n, displacement)
        self._loss = jax.jit(loss)
        self._grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss, has_aux=True))

    def _checked(self, f, x):
        out, nbrs = f(x, self.nbrs)
        if nbrs.did_buffer_overflow:  # host sync, as in jax-md's examples
            self.nbrs = self.neighbor_fn.allocate(x)
            out, nbrs = f(x, self.nbrs)
        self.nbrs = nbrs
        return out

    def loss(self, x):
        return self._checked(self._loss, x)

    def grad(self, x):
        return self._checked(self._grad, x)


P0 = Particles(x0)
g = P0.grad(x0)
print(f"loss = {float(P0.loss(x0)):.10f}   ‖∇loss‖ = {float(jnp.linalg.norm(g)):.6f}")

# loops in device `malloc` memory. CUDA's default device heap is 8 MB, which overflows
# above ~30k particles (illegal memory access). Must be set before the first kernel.
CUDA.limit!(CUDA.LIMIT_MALLOC_HEAP_SIZE, 2^32)

# The whole pipeline is differentiated: cell ids, counting sort, gather into sorted
# order, and neighbour loops whose ranges depend on the data.
function sph_loss(x::AbstractMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    s, rc = p.L / nc, 2 * p.h

    # 1. cell id of every particle, and particles per cell
    cell  = Vector{Int}(undef, N)
    start = zeros(Int, nc * nc + 1)
    @inbounds for i in 1:N
        cx = mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc)
        cy = mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)
        cell[i] = 1 + cx + nc * cy
        start[cell[i] + 1] += 1
    end

    # 2. counting sort by cell: start[c] is the first sorted index of cell c
    start[1] = 1
    for c in 1:nc * nc
        start[c + 1] += start[c]
    end
    cursor = start[1:end-1]
    perm = Vector{Int}(undef, N)
    @inbounds for i in 1:N
        perm[cursor[cell[i]]] = i
        cursor[cell[i]] += 1
    end

    # 3. gather positions into sorted order: each cell is contiguous in memory
    xs = similar(x)
    @inbounds for k in 1:N
        xs[1, k] = x[1, perm[k]]
        xs[2, k] = x[2, perm[k]]
    end

    # 4. density and loss over the 3×3 neighbouring cells; each cell is the range
    #    start[c]:start[c+1]-1, whose length depends on the data
    loss = zero(T)
    @inbounds for k in 1:N
        c = cell[perm[k]] - 1
        cx, cy = c % nc, c ÷ nc
        ρ = zero(T)
        for dy in -1:1, dx in -1:1
            cn = 1 + mod(cx + dx, nc) + nc * mod(cy + dy, nc)
            for l in start[cn]:start[cn + 1] - 1
                rx = minimg(xs[1, k] - xs[1, l], p.L)
                ry = minimg(xs[2, k] - xs[2, l], p.L)
                r2 = rx * rx + ry * ry
                if r2 < rc * rc
                    ρ += p.m * W(sqrt(r2), p.h)
                end
            end
        end
        loss += (ρ - p.ρ0)^2
    end
    return loss
end

sph_loss (generic function with 1 method)



function sph_gradient(x::Matrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    dx = zero(x)
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, sph_loss, Active, Duplicated(x, dx), Const(p))
    return dx
end

# Same algorithm as KernelAbstractions kernels. The cell list is integer-valued (zero
# derivative), so it is built outside the differentiated function with CUDA.jl's sort.
# The gather and the neighbour loops are differentiated.

# Box size, smoothing length etc. are not differentiated; declaring that lets Params be
# passed to GPU kernels, which reject active (differentiable) scalar arguments.
Enzyme.EnzymeRules.inactive_type(::Type{<:Params}) = true

@kernel function cell_ids!(cell, counts, @Const(x), s, nc)
    i = @index(Global)
    @inbounds begin
        cx = mod(unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(x[1, i] / s)), Int32(nc))
        cy = mod(unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(x[2, i] / s)), Int32(nc))
        cell[i] = Int32(1) + cx + Int32(nc) * cy
        KernelAbstractions.@atomic counts[cell[i] + 1] += Int32(1)
    end
end

function build_cells(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    cell = CuVector{Int32}(undef, N)
    counts = CUDA.zeros(Int32, nc * nc + 1)
    cell_ids!(get_backend(x))(cell, counts, x, p.L / nc, nc; ndrange=N)
    counts[1:1] .= 1
    perm = sortperm(cell)
    return (; perm=Int32.(perm), cell=cell[perm], start=cumsum(counts))
end

@kernel function gather!(xs, @Const(x), @Const(perm))
    k = @index(Global)
    @inbounds xs[1, k] = x[1, perm[k]]
    @inbounds xs[2, k] = x[2, perm[k]]
end

@kernel function density_loss!(e, @Const(xs), @Const(cellk), @Const(start), p)
    k = @index(Global)
    T, nc = eltype(xs), Int32(p.nc)
    @inbounds begin
        c = cellk[k] - Int32(1)
        cx, cy = c % nc, c ÷ nc
        ρ = zero(T)
        for dy in Int32(-1):Int32(1), dx in Int32(-1):Int32(1)
            cn = Int32(1) + mod(cx + dx, nc) + nc * mod(cy + dy, nc)
            for l in start[cn]:start[cn + 1] - Int32(1)      # data-dependent range
                rx = minimg(xs[1, k] - xs[1, l], p.L)
                ry = minimg(xs[2, k] - xs[2, l], p.L)
                r2 = rx * rx + ry * ry
                if r2 < 4 * p.h * p.h
                    ρ += p.m * W(sqrt(r2), p.h)
                end
            end
        end
        e[k] = (ρ - p.ρ0)^2
    end
end

"Per-particle loss terms e (in sorted order); the loss is sum(e)."
function sph_terms!(e, xs, x, cells, p)
    backend, N = get_backend(x), size(x, 2)
    gather!(backend)(xs, x, cells.perm; ndrange=N)
    density_loss!(backend)(e, xs, cells.cell, cells.start, p; ndrange=N)
    return nothing
end

function sph_loss(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    e, xs = similar(x, size(x, 2)), similar(x)
    sph_terms!(e, xs, x, build_cells(x, p), p)
    return sum(e)
end

"Gradient of sum(e): reverse mode seeded with de = 1."
function sph_gradient(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N = size(x, 2)
    e, de = similar(x, N), CUDA.ones(T, N)
    xs, dxs = similar(x), CUDA.zeros(T, size(x))
    dx = CUDA.zeros(T, size(x))
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, sph_terms!, Const,
                    Duplicated(e, de), Duplicated(xs, dxs), Duplicated(x, dx),
                    Const(build_cells(x, p)), Const(p))
    return dx
end

title: 01. Particles: sort, cell lists, and data-dependent neighbour loops
text:
\(N\) particles in a periodic square box, each with an SPH density \[\rho_i = \sum_j m\, W(\lVert x_i - x_j\rVert, h),\] where \(W\) is the 2D cubic-spline kernel with support \(2h\), and the loss \[\mathcal{L}(x) = \sum_i (\rho_i - \rho_0)^2 .\] We want \(\nabla_x \mathcal{L}\), the gradient with respect to all particle positions. The box grows with \(N\) so every particle has about 31 neighbours.
This loss came up in a Slack discussion as “something JAX can’t do because it needs sort!”. That is not quite right: jax.lax.sort is differentiable. What matters is how the efficient algorithm works:

compute each particle’s cell (integer, zero derivative),

The Enzyme version is the algorithm above as plain loops, differentiated as written: on the CPU the whole pipeline, including the counting sort, is inside autodiff. JAX and Reactant cannot express step 3 (a loop whose bounds come from the data), so they regularise it. JAX uses jax-md’s padded neighbour list; Reactant uses a padded cell list. # The whole pipeline is differentiated: cell ids, counting sort, gather into sorted
# order, and neighbour loops whose ranges depend on the data.
function sph_loss(x::AbstractMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    s, rc = p.L / nc, 2 * p.h

    # 1. cell id of every particle, and particles per cell
    cell  = Vector{Int}(undef, N)
    start = zeros(Int, nc * nc + 1)
    @inbounds for i in 1:N
        cx = mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc)
        cy = mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)
        cell[i] = 1 + cx + nc * cy
        start[cell[i] + 1] += 1
    end

    # 2. counting sort by cell: start[c] is the first sorted index of cell c
    start[1] = 1
    for c in 1:nc * nc
        start[c + 1] += start[c]
    end
    cursor = start[1:end-1]
    perm = Vector{Int}(undef, N)
    @inbounds for i in 1:N
        perm[cursor[cell[i]]] = i
        cursor[cell[i]] += 1
    end

    # 3. gather positions into sorted order: each cell is contiguous in memory
    xs = similar(x)
    @inbounds for k in 1:N
        xs[1, k] = x[1, perm[k]]
        xs[2, k] = x[2, perm[k]]
    end

    # 4. density and loss over the 3×3 neighbouring cells; each cell is the range
    #    start[c]:start[c+1]-1, whose length depends on the data
    loss = zero(T)
    @inbounds for k in 1:N
        c = cell[perm[k]] - 1
        cx, cy = c % nc, c ÷ nc
        ρ = zero(T)
        for dy in -1:1, dx in -1:1
            cn = 1 + mod(cx + dx, nc) + nc * mod(cy + dy, nc)
            for l in start[cn]:start[cn + 1] - 1
                rx = minimg(xs[1, k] - xs[1, l], p.L)
                ry = minimg(xs[2, k] - xs[2, l], p.L)
                r2 = rx * rx + ry * ry
                if r2 < rc * rc
                    ρ += p.m * W(sqrt(r2), p.h)
                end
            end
        end
        loss += (ρ - p.ρ0)^2
    end
    return loss
end

@kernel function cell_ids!(cell, counts, @Const(x), s, nc)
    i = @index(Global)
    @inbounds begin
        cx = mod(unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(x[1, i] / s)), Int32(nc))
        cy = mod(unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(x[2, i] / s)), Int32(nc))
        cell[i] = Int32(1) + cx + Int32(nc) * cy
        KernelAbstractions.@atomic counts[cell[i] + 1] += Int32(1)
    end

function build_cells(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc

    counts = CUDA.zeros(Int32, nc * nc + 1)
    cell_ids!(get_backend(x))(cell, counts, x, p.L / nc, nc; ndrange=N)
    counts[1:1] .= 1
    perm = sortperm(cell)
    return (; perm=Int32.(perm), cell=cell[perm], start=cumsum(counts))
end

@kernel function gather!(xs, @Const(x), @Const(perm))
    k = @index(Global)
    @inbounds xs[1, k] = x[1, perm[k]]
    @inbounds xs[2, k] = x[2, perm[k]]
end

@kernel function density_loss!(e, @Const(xs), @Const(cellk), @Const(start), p)
    k = @index(Global)
    T, nc = eltype(xs), Int32(p.nc)
    @inbounds begin
        c = cellk[k] - Int32(1)
        cx, cy = c % nc, c ÷ nc
        ρ = zero(T)
        for dy in Int32(-1):Int32(1), dx in Int32(-1):Int32(1)
            cn = Int32(1) + mod(cx + dx, nc) + nc * mod(cy + dy, nc)
            for l in start[cn]:start[cn + 1] - Int32(1)      # data-dependent range
                rx = minimg(xs[1, k] - xs[1, l], p.L)
                ry = minimg(xs[2, k] - xs[2, l], p.L)
                r2 = rx * rx + ry * ry
                if r2 < 4 * p.h * p.h
                    ρ += p.m * W(sqrt(r2), p.h)
                end
            end
        end
        e[k] = (ρ - p.ρ0)^2
    end
end

"Per-particle loss terms e (in sorted order); the loss is sum(e)."
function sph_terms!(e, xs, x, cells, p)
    backend, N = get_backend(x), size(x, 2)
    gather!(backend)(xs, x, cells.perm; ndrange=N)
    density_loss!(backend)(e, xs, cells.cell, cells.start, p; ndrange=N)
    return nothing
end

    e, xs = similar(x, size(x, 2)), similar(x)

# Reactant traces Julia array code into one XLA program, so it has JAX's constraints:
# static shapes, no data-dependent loop bounds, no branches on traced values. The cell
# list is regularised like a padded JAX cell list: every neighbour cell is read
# through `cap` slots and slots past the cell's end are masked.

# `W` from common.jl branches (`if q < 1`), which cannot be traced. Select instead,
# evaluating both polynomials for every pair, as JAX's `jnp.where` does.
@inline function W_select(r, h::T) where {T}
    q = r / h
    σ = T(10) / (T(7) * T(π) * h * h)
    t = max(2 - q, zero(T))
    return σ * ifelse(q < 1, 1 - T(1.5) * q * q + T(0.75) * q * q * q, T(0.25) * t * t * t)
end

"""
First sorted index of each cell, using only sorts and gathers: merge the sorted cell
ids (keys 2c) with one probe per cell (keys 2c−1); the rank of probe c, minus the
c−1 probes before it, is the start of cell c.
"""
function cell_starts(cs, ncells)
    N = length(cs)
    probes = 2 .* Int32.(1:ncells+1) .- Int32(1)
    order = sortperm(vcat(2 .* cs, Reactant.promote_to(typeof(cs), probes)))
    rank = sortperm(order)                       # inverse permutation
    return rank[N+1:end] .- Int32.(0:ncells)
end

function sph_loss_padded(x::AbstractMatrix, p::Params{T}, ::Val{cap}) where {T,cap}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    s = p.L / nc

    cell = Int32(1) .+ mod.(floor.(Int32, x[1, :] ./ s), Int32(nc)) .+
           Int32(nc) .* mod.(floor.(Int32, x[2, :] ./ s), Int32(nc))
    perm = sortperm(cell)
    cs = cell[perm]
    start = cell_starts(cs, nc * nc)
    xs, ys = x[1, perm], x[2, perm]
    cxs, cys = (cs .- Int32(1)) .% Int32(nc), (cs .- Int32(1)) .÷ Int32(nc)
    slots = reshape(Int32.(0:cap-1), cap, 1)

    ρ = zero(xs)
    for dy in -1:1, dx in -1:1                   # unrolled at trace time
        cn = Int32(1) .+ mod.(cxs .+ Int32(dx), Int32(nc)) .+
             Int32(nc) .* mod.(cys .+ Int32(dy), Int32(nc))
        idx = reshape(start[cn], 1, N) .+ slots                  # (cap, N) candidates
        valid = idx .< reshape(start[cn .+ Int32(1)], 1, N)
        l = clamp.(idx, Int32(1), Int32(N))
        rx = minimg.(reshape(xs, 1, N) .- xs[l], p.L)
        ry = minimg.(reshape(ys, 1, N) .- ys[l], p.L)
        r2 = rx .^ 2 .+ ry .^ 2
        inside = valid .& (r2 .< 4 * p.h * p.h)
        r = sqrt.(ifelse.(inside, r2, one(T)))  # keep sqrt' finite on masked slots
        ρ = ρ .+ vec(sum(ifelse.(inside, p.m .* W_select.(r, p.h), zero(T)); dims=1))
    end
    return sum((ρ .- p.ρ0) .^ 2)
end

"Capacity needed: the largest cell occupancy. Too small silently drops neighbours."
function max_occupancy(x, p)
    s, nc = p.L / p.nc, p.nc
    counts = zeros(Int, nc * nc)
    for i in axes(x, 2)
        counts[1 + mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc) + nc * mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)] += 1
    end
    return maximum(counts)
end

# Idiomatic JAX: jax-md's neighbour list. It is a fixed-capacity padded pair list;
# `allocate` (outside jit) sizes it from the data, `update` (inside jit) refills it,
# and `did_buffer_overflow` must be checked after every call.
NUMBER_DENSITY, H, MASS = 10.0, 0.5, 1.0
RC, RHO0 = 2 * H, NUMBER_DENSITY

def box_size(n):
    return math.sqrt(n / NUMBER_DENSITY)

def W(r, h=H):
    """2D cubic spline. No `if`: both branches are evaluated and selected."""
    q = r / h
    sigma = 10.0 / (7.0 * math.pi * h * h)
    t = jnp.maximum(2.0 - q, 0.0)
    return sigma * jnp.where(q < 1.0, 1.0 - 1.5 * q**2 + 0.75 * q**3, 0.25 * t**3)

def make_loss(n, displacement):
    w0 = MASS * float(W(0.0))  # self-contribution; jax-md's pair list excludes i == j

    def loss(x, nbrs):
        nbrs = nbrs.update(x)  # rebuild the cell list from the current positions
        i, j = nbrs.idx
        mask = i < n  # padded slots hold index n
        dR = jax.vmap(displacement)(x[i], x[j])
        dR = jnp.where(mask[:, None], dR, 1.0)  # padded dR = 0 would make ∇‖dR‖ NaN
        r = jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(dR**2, axis=1))
        w = jnp.where(mask, MASS * W(r), 0.0)
        rho = w0 + jax.ops.segment_sum(w, i, num_segments=n)
        return jnp.sum((rho - RHO0) ** 2), nbrs

    return loss

class Particles:
    """Jitted loss and gradient with jax-md's overflow-and-reallocate protocol."""

    def __init__(self, x, capacity_multiplier=1.25):
        self.n = x.shape[0]
        L = box_size(self.n)
        displacement, _ = space.periodic(L)
        self.neighbor_fn = partition.neighbor_list(
            displacement, L, RC, dr_threshold=0.0,
            capacity_multiplier=capacity_multiplier, format=partition.Sparse)
        self.nbrs = self.neighbor_fn.allocate(x)
        loss = make_loss(self.n, displacement)
        self._loss = jax.jit(loss)
        self._grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss, has_aux=True))

    def _checked(self, f, x):
        out, nbrs = f(x, self.nbrs)
        if nbrs.did_buffer_overflow:  # host sync, as in jax-md's examples
            self.nbrs = self.neighbor_fn.allocate(x)
            out, nbrs = f(x, self.nbrs)
        self.nbrs = nbrs
        return out

    def loss(self, x):
        return self._checked(self._loss, x)

    def grad(self, x):
        return self._checked(self._grad, x)

text:
What this shows
Differentiating the irregular algorithm works. Enzyme differentiates the mutating, sort-based, data-dependent loop code directly and gets the same gradient as JAX and Reactant to machine precision. No padding, no capacity, no overflow check, no where tricks to keep sqrt finite. On the CPU at \(N = 10^6\), single-threaded Enzyme takes 4.78 s for the gradient, against 5.98 s for multithreaded JAX. The forward pass alone takes 1.42 s against 5.46 s.
The padded version runs out of memory on the GPU. In Float64, jax-md’s neighbour list for \(10^6\) particles does not fit on the 16 GB GPU: building it needs a further 4 GiB intermediate on top of a pair list of 39 million slots. Enzyme’s cell list needs no capacity at all.
Reactant behaves like JAX. Reactant is Julia, but compiled through XLA, and it needs the same regularisation: padded cells, masks, a branch-free kernel. At \(N = 10^5\) its gradient takes 21.1 ms against JAX’s 10.3 ms. Its padded cell list is leaner than jax-md’s pair list (no stored pair indices), so it still fits at \(N = 10^6\) (196.1 ms). The constraint comes from the static-graph execution model, not from the language.

section: Where JAX wins / where Enzyme hurts
text:
Where JAX wins / where Enzyme hurts






WarningOn the GPU, today, the padded versions are much faster than Enzyme’s



At \(N = 10^5\) the Enzyme GPU gradient takes 119.1 ms, against 10.3 ms for JAX and 21.1 ms for Reactant. At \(N = 10^6\) it takes 2.57 s, 84× its own forward pass.
The reason is how Enzyme compiles reverse-mode GPU kernels with a data-dependent inner loop: it stores values for every inner iteration in device malloc memory, in both the augmented forward kernel and the reverse kernel. With CUDA’s default 8 MB device heap this crashes above about 30 000 particles, so the notebook raises the heap to 4 GiB. A branch-free kernel and a fixed-trip-count kernel showed the same behaviour.


What we did not do:

No hand-written adjoint on either side. A JAX expert could write the neighbour loop as a Pallas kernel with a hand-written backward pass. An Enzyme user could restructure the GPU gradient as a forward kernel plus a gather kernel that applies Enzyme only to the scalar pair function. Both are faster, and both give up “the adjoint for free”.
No multithreaded Enzyme CPU version. The CPU numbers are single-threaded Julia against multithreaded XLA.

        inside = valid .& (r2 .< 4 * p.h * p.h)
        r = sqrt.(ifelse.(inside, r2, one(T)))  # keep sqrt' finite on masked slots
        ρ = ρ .+ vec(sum(ifelse.(inside, p.m .* W_select.(r, p.h), zero(T)); dims=1))
    end
    return sum((ρ .- p.ρ0) .^ 2)
end

"Capacity needed: the largest cell occupancy. Too small silently drops neighbours."
function max_occupancy(x, p)
    s, nc = p.L / p.nc, p.nc
    counts = zeros(Int, nc * nc)
    for i in axes(x, 2)
        counts[1 + mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc) + nc * mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)] += 1
    end
    return maximum(counts)
end

title: 02. Gauss–Seidel: a sequential in-place sweep
text:
Solve \(-\Delta u = \theta\) on the unit square (\(n \times n\) interior points, \(u = 0\) on the boundary) with \(K\) Gauss–Seidel sweeps from \(u = 0\), and differentiate \[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \lVert u_K(\theta) - u_{\text{obs}} \rVert^2\] with respect to the source \(\theta\). Each update is \[u_{ij} \leftarrow \tfrac14\left(h^2\theta_{ij} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i+1,j} + u_{i,j-1} + u_{i,j+1}\right),\] in place: \(u_{i-1,j}\) and \(u_{i,j-1}\) are values already updated earlier in the same sweep. That is what makes Gauss–Seidel converge about twice as fast as Jacobi, and it is what makes it a sequential loop.
The same pattern appears in SOR, incomplete factorisations, the Thomas algorithm, upwind sweeps and line relaxation.
Two variants:

Lexicographic, the textbook sweep: a triple loop.
Red-black, which colours the grid like a chessboard so that each colour can be updated in parallel. It is a different iteration, with a different result, and it is the formulation a GPU or JAX user writes. Gradients are compared within each variant.

# Lexicographic Gauss–Seidel, in place: u[i, j] uses the *new* u[i-1, j] and u[i, j-1].
function gs_loss(θ::AbstractMatrix{T}, uobs, K) where {T}
    n = size(θ, 1)
    h2 = one(T) / (n + 1)^2
    u = zeros(T, n + 2, n + 2)
    for _ in 1:K, j in 2:n+1, i in 2:n+1
        u[i, j] = (h2 * θ[i-1, j-1] + u[i-1, j] + u[i+1, j] + u[i, j-1] + u[i, j+1]) / 4
    end
    loss = zero(T)
    for j in 1:n, i in 1:n
        loss += (u[i+1, j+1] - uobs[i, j])^2
    end
    return loss
end

# Red-black Gauss–Seidel as a KernelAbstractions kernel (runs on CPU and GPU): points
# of one colour read only the other colour, so all threads of a colour are independent.
@kernel function rb_half_sweep!(u, @Const(θ), colour)
    I = @index(Global, Cartesian)
    i, j = I[1] + 1, I[2] + 1
    h2 = one(eltype(u)) / (size(θ, 1) + 1)^2   # computed here: GPU kernels take no active scalars
    @inbounds if (i + j) % 2 == colour
        u[i, j] = (h2 * θ[i-1, j-1] + u[i-1, j] + u[i+1, j] + u[i, j-1] + u[i, j+1]) / 4
    end
end

@kernel function sqdiff!(e, @Const(u), @Const(uobs))
    I = @index(Global, Cartesian)
    @inbounds e[I] = (u[I[1]+1, I[2]+1] - uobs[I])^2
end

function rb_terms!(e, u, θ, uobs, K)
    backend, n = get_backend(u), size(θ, 1)
    fill!(u, 0)
    for _ in 1:K, colour in (0, 1)
        rb_half_sweep!(backend)(u, θ, colour; ndrange=(n, n))
    end
    sqdiff!(backend)(e, u, uobs; ndrange=(n, n))
    return nothing
end

function rb_loss(θ, uobs, K)
    n = size(θ, 1)
    e, u = similar(θ), similar(θ, n + 2, n + 2)
    rb_terms!(e, u, θ, uobs, K)
    return sum(e)
end

# Lexicographic Gauss–Seidel. Arrays are immutable and loop bodies must be pure, so
# the sweep is a scan over columns, each a scan over rows carrying the new u[i-1, j].
# Same update order as the Julia loop (i fastest, then j).
@functools.partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=2)
def gs_loss(theta, uobs, K):
    n = theta.shape[0]
    h2 = 1.0 / (n + 1) ** 2

    def column(u, j):
        left, old, right = u[:, j], u[:, j + 1], u[:, j + 2]

        def point(below, i):  # below = new u[i-1, j]
            new = (h2 * theta[i, j] + below + old[i + 2] + left[i + 1] + right[i + 1]) / 4
            return new, new

        _, col = jax.lax.scan(point, old[0], jnp.arange(n))
        return u.at[1:n + 1, j + 1].set(col), None

    def sweep(u, _):
        return jax.lax.scan(column, u, jnp.arange(n))[0], None

    u, _ = jax.lax.scan(sweep, jnp.zeros((n + 2, n + 2), theta.dtype), None, length=K)
    return jnp.sum((u[1:-1, 1:-1] - uobs) ** 2)

# Red-black Gauss–Seidel: the reformulation JAX users actually write. Each colour is
# one vectorised stencil, selected with a mask.
@functools.partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=2)
def rb_loss(theta, uobs, K):
    n = theta.shape[0]
    h2 = 1.0 / (n + 1) ** 2
    i, j = jnp.meshgrid(jnp.arange(2, n + 2), jnp.arange(2, n + 2), indexing="ij")
    red = (i + j) % 2 == 0  # 1-based indices, as in the Julia kernel

    def half(u, colour):
        new = (h2 * theta + u[:-2, 1:-1] + u[2:, 1:-1] + u[1:-1, :-2] + u[1:-1, 2:]) / 4
        return u.at[1:-1, 1:-1].set(jnp.where(colour, new, u[1:-1, 1:-1]))

    def sweep(u, _):
        return half(half(u, red), ~red), None

    u, _ = jax.lax.scan(sweep, jnp.zeros((n + 2, n + 2), theta.dtype), None, length=K)
    return jnp.sum((u[1:-1, 1:-1] - uobs) ** 2)

title: 02. Gauss–Seidel: a sequential in-place sweep
text:
What this shows
The sequential sweep on the CPU. At \(n = 512\) the lexicographic gradient takes 325.7 ms with Enzyme and 19.7 s with JAX, although their forward passes are close (177.6 ms and 517.8 ms). Enzyme’s gradient costs 1.8× its forward pass; JAX’s costs 38×. JAX expresses the sweep as nested lax.scans, and the transposed scan of a scan does much more work per step than the scalar loop it came from.
The sequential sweep on the GPU. At \(n = 64\) the lexicographic gradient takes 7.3 s with JAX and 8.3 s with Reactant, against 4.1 ms for Enzyme on one CPU core. Every scalar update becomes a step of an XLA loop, which on the GPU means a device round trip per grid point. Reactant traces the same Julia triple loop as Enzyme, so the language is not the issue: the loop is slow once it goes through XLA.
Memory does not grow with K, for either tool. We expected reverse mode through \(K\) in-place sweeps to store \(K\) copies of \(u\). It doesn’t, because each update is linear: its derivative is the constant \(\tfrac14\), so the backward pass needs no stored values. Both Enzyme’s activity analysis and JAX’s linearisation see this.

section: Where JAX wins / what we did not do

Where JAX wins / what we did not do






Note



Red-black on the GPU is where the XLA tools shine. At \(n = 1024\) the red-black gradient takes 16.8 ms with Reactant, 20.0 ms with JAX and 21.9 ms with Enzyme through KernelAbstractions; on small grids Enzyme is several times slower. Enzyme launches two kernels per sweep, forward and reverse, while XLA compiles the whole loop into one program. That launch overhead dominates on small grids.



A JAX expert can rewrite the lexicographic sweep without a scalar loop. Along each column the update is a first-order linear recurrence, which jax.lax.associative_scan evaluates in parallel. That is a different algorithm, with different rounding and \(O(\log n)\) depth, and you have to know the trick.
No Enzyme multithreading and no fused multi-sweep GPU kernel.

title: 03. Compaction and scatter-add: work proportional to the data
text:
\(N\) particles move with fixed velocities on the periodic interval \([0, 1)\). At each of \(T = 50\) steps, a narrow window sweeps across the domain. The particles inside it, about 1 %, are deposited with linear (cloud-in-cell) weights into a histogram \(H\) of 1024 bins. A taper \(w(d) = (1 - |d|/h_w)^2\) fades the contribution to zero at the window edges, which keeps the loss differentiable as particles enter and leave. We differentiate \[\mathcal{L}(x_0) = \lVert H(x_0) - H_{\text{target}} \rVert^2\] with respect to the initial positions.
Two irregular patterns are involved:

Compaction. The work worth doing is proportional to the number of selected particles, which changes with the data: x[mask], findall, push! into a buffer.
Scatter-add at data-dependent indices: H[j] += w.

The same patterns appear in event detection, active-set methods, particle-in-cell deposits, histogramming, and resampling.

function deposit_loss(x0::Vector{T}, v, target, s::Setup) where {T}
    N, nb = length(x0), s.nb
    H = zeros(T, nb)
    sel = Int[]                                   # grows and shrinks with the data
    for t in 1:s.T
        c = T(t) / s.T                            # window centre
        empty!(sel)
        for i in 1:N                              # compaction: indices of x[mask]
            d = minimg(x0[i] + v[i] * (t * s.dt) - c)
            abs(d) < s.halfwidth && push!(sel, i)
        end
        for i in sel                              # work only for the selected particles
            x = wrap(x0[i] + v[i] * (t * s.dt))
            w = taper(minimg(x - c), s.halfwidth)
            g = x * nb - T(0.5)                   # cloud-in-cell deposit
            j = floor(Int, g)
            f = g - j
            H[mod(j, nb) + 1] += w * (1 - f)      # scatter-add at a data-dependent index
            H[mod(j + 1, nb) + 1] += w * f
        end
    end
    return sum(abs2, H .- target)
end

def minimg(d):
    return d - jnp.round(d)

def taper(d):
    return jnp.maximum(1.0 - jnp.abs(d) / HW, 0.0) ** 2

def deposit(H, x, w):
    """Cloud-in-cell scatter-add into the histogram."""
    g = x * NB - 0.5
    j = jnp.floor(g).astype(jnp.int32)
    f = g - j
    return H.at[j % NB].add(w * (1 - f)).at[(j + 1) % NB].add(w * f)

# Masked: every particle is deposited at every step, with weight 0 outside the window.
@jax.jit
def loss_masked(x0, v, target):
    def step(H, t):
        x = x0 + v * (t * DT)
        d = minimg(x - t / T)
        w = jnp.where(jnp.abs(d) < HW, taper(d), 0.0)
        return deposit(H, x - jnp.floor(x), w), None
    H, _ = jax.lax.scan(step, jnp.zeros(NB, x0.dtype), jnp.arange(1, T + 1))
    return jnp.sum((H - target) ** 2)

# Compacted: the closest JAX gets to x[mask]. `nonzero` needs a static `size`, so the
# selection is padded to a capacity chosen from the data, checked outside jit.
@functools.partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=3)
def loss_compact(x0, v, target, cap):
    n = x0.shape[0]
    def step(H, t):
        inside = jnp.abs(minimg(x0 + v * (t * DT) - t / T)) < HW
        idx = jnp.nonzero(inside, size=cap, fill_value=n)[0]
        i = jnp.minimum(idx, n - 1)
        x = x0[i] + v[i] * (t * DT)
        w = jnp.where(idx < n, taper(minimg(x - t / T)), 0.0)
        return deposit(H, x - jnp.floor(x), w), None
    H, _ = jax.lax.scan(step, jnp.zeros(NB, x0.dtype), jnp.arange(1, T + 1))
    return jnp.sum((H - target) ** 2)

def needed_capacity(x0, v):
    """Largest number of selected particles at any step (host-side, outside jit)."""
    t = np.arange(1, T + 1)[:, None]
    d = np.asarray(x0)[None] + np.asarray(v)[None] * t * DT - t / T
    return int((np.abs(d - np.round(d)) < HW).sum(axis=1).max())

"Residual F(u, θ) = A u + u³ − θ with zero Dirichlet ends, written into F."
function residual!(F, u, θ)
    n = length(u)
    ih2 = (n + 1)^2
    for i in 1:n
        l = i > 1 ? u[i-1] : zero(eltype(u))
        r = i < n ? u[i+1] : zero(eltype(u))
        F[i] = ih2 * (2u[i] - l - r) + u[i]^3 - θ[i]
    end
end

"Solve J δ = F in place (δ overwrites F), J = A + 3 diag(u²): the Thomas algorithm."
function thomas!(F, c, u)
    n = length(u)
    ih2 = (n + 1)^2
    off = -ih2
    b = 2ih2 + 3u[1]^2
    c[1] = off / b
    F[1] = F[1] / b
    for i in 2:n                                  # forward elimination
        b = 2ih2 + 3u[i]^2 - off * c[i-1]
        c[i] = off / b
        F[i] = (F[i] - off * F[i-1]) / b
    end
    for i in n-1:-1:1                             # back substitution
        F[i] -= c[i] * F[i+1]
    end
end

"Newton until the step is small; returns the solution and the iteration count."
function newton_solve(θ::AbstractVector{T}) where {T}
    n = length(θ)
    u, F, c = zeros(T, n), zeros(T, n), zeros(T, n)
    it, converged = 0, false
    while !converged && it < MAXITER              # data-dependent trip count
        residual!(F, u, θ)
        thomas!(F, c, u)                          # F now holds the Newton step δ
        u .-= F
        it += 1
        converged = maximum(abs, F) <= TOL * maximum(abs, u)
    end
    return u, it
end

import numpy as np
import weanj  # sets XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false before JAX initialises
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import lineax as lx
import optimistix as optx

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
EXAMPLE, TOL, MAXITER = "04-newton", 1e-10, 50
d = weanj.load_inputs(EXAMPLE)
theta0, uobs0 = jnp.asarray(d["theta"]), jnp.asarray(d["uobs"])


def residual(u, theta):
    n = u.shape[0]
    ih2 = (n + 1) ** 2
    up = jnp.pad(u, 1)
    return ih2 * (2 * u - up[:-2] - up[2:]) + u**3 - theta

def newton_step(u, theta):
    n = u.shape[0]
    ih2 = (n + 1) ** 2
    lower = jnp.full(n, -ih2, u.dtype).at[0].set(0.0)
    upper = jnp.full(n, -ih2, u.dtype).at[-1].set(0.0)
    diag = 2 * ih2 + 3 * u**2
    delta = jax.lax.linalg.tridiagonal_solve(lower, diag, upper, residual(u, theta)[:, None])[:, 0]
    return u - delta

# The direct translation: Newton until the step is small.
def loss_while(theta, uobs):
    def cond(state):
        u, step, it = state
        return (step > TOL * jnp.max(jnp.abs(u))) & (it < MAXITER)
    def body(state):
        u, _, it = state
        u_new = newton_step(u, theta)
        return u_new, jnp.max(jnp.abs(u_new - u)), it + 1
    u, _, _ = jax.lax.while_loop(cond, body, (jnp.zeros_like(theta), jnp.inf, 0))
    return jnp.sum((u - uobs) ** 2)

# Workaround 1: a fixed number of Newton steps, enough for the worst case.
def loss_fixed(theta, uobs, iters=MAXITER):
    u = jax.lax.fori_loop(0, iters, lambda _, u: newton_step(u, theta), jnp.zeros_like(theta))
    return jnp.sum((u - uobs) ** 2)

# Workaround 2 (idiomatic): Optimistix root finding, differentiated implicitly.
def loss_implicit(theta, uobs):
    # Optimistix stops when the step is small *and* |F| < atol. Rounding in F grows like
    # (n+1)²·eps, so we root-find on h²·F instead: same root, same Newton steps, same
    # implicit gradient, but a residual whose rounding error is ~eps·|u|.
    def scaled_residual(u, theta):
        return residual(u, theta) / (u.shape[0] + 1) ** 2
    solver = optx.Newton(rtol=TOL, atol=1e-12, linear_solver=lx.Tridiagonal())
    sol = optx.root_find(scaled_residual, solver, jnp.zeros_like(theta), theta,
                         tags=frozenset({lx.tridiagonal_tag}), max_steps=MAXITER)
    return jnp.sum((sol.value - uobs) ** 2)


try:
    jax.grad(loss_while)(theta0, uobs0)
except ValueError as err:
    print("jax.grad(loss_while):", str(err).splitlines()[0])

grad_fixed = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss_fixed))
grad_implicit = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss_implicit))

title: Methodology
text: How the comparisons are made, so they can be checked and reproduced.

title: Methodology
text:
Same inputs
Inputs for each example are generated once in Julia with a fixed seed and written to data/<example>.npz. All three implementations load that file.

title: Methodology
text:
Same gradient
Every implementation computes the gradient of the same loss at the same point in Float64 and saves it to benchmarks/grads/<example>_<impl>.npz. Each example page checks that

every gradient agrees with central finite differences on a few random components, and
all three gradients agree with each other (relative tolerance 1e-8).

A failing check fails the build, so a published page always shows matching gradients.

title: Methodology
text:
Timing

Everything runs in Float64, timing included, so the timed code is exactly the code whose gradient was checked. The laptop GPU used here has low Float64 throughput (as most consumer GPUs do), which slows every GPU column; relative comparisons between GPU columns are what matter.
Compile time (first call) is reported separately from run time. It matters for JAX and Reactant, which compile a whole graph, and for Enzyme, which compiles on first call.
Run time is the median of 10 calls after 2 warm-up calls. GPU work is synchronised inside the timed region (CUDA.synchronize, jax.block_until_ready).
Problem size N is swept over several orders of magnitude so scaling is visible, not just one data point.
Peak device memory is reported where the tool exposes it.
Benchmarks run on an otherwise idle GPU (make gpu-check refuses to run otherwise).

title: Methodology
section: Fairness rules for the JAX column
text:
Fairness rules for the JAX column
The JAX code is what a competent JAX user would write, not a literal translation:

jax.jit everything, donate buffers where it helps, and use jax.checkpoint where a practitioner would.
Use the ecosystem’s own tools where they exist: jax-md cell and neighbour lists, Optimistix for implicit differentiation, Diffrax for adaptive time stepping.
Where JAX needs a static capacity (padding), size it from the data and handle overflow the way jax-md does, and report the padding overhead.
Every example page has a “Where JAX wins / what we did not do” note.

title: Methodology
text:
Hardware and software
Results on the published site were produced on an NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada Generation Laptop GPU (16 GB), Julia 1.12, Enzyme.jl 0.13, Reactant.jl 0.2, JAX 0.11 (CUDA 13). Exact versions are pinned in julia/Manifest.toml and python/uv.lock.
